newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Budget Bills - Status Overview.
newsitem.headline: Australian Budget Bills - Status Overview.

text.p: Here is a review of the status of the Australian government's budget measures.
Each measure is described with, where available, a brief rundown on its status in the legislative process.
The values of each measure to the budget are shown, first for 1997/98 and then 1998/99. ---------------------
REVENUE MEASURES:

TAX REBATE ON SAVINGS -- Tax concessions for savings, with costs to revenue that offset lower spending from the abolition of the planned government contribution to retirement savings. Assistant Treasurer Rod Kemp's office is unsure at this stage as to whether there will be a separate bill for this measure or whether it will be contained in various superannuation bills.
Impact on revenue: Zero, minus A$350

SUPERANNUATION PRESERVATION & OTHER SUPERANNUATION MEASURES -- These measures will not be introduced until July 1998, so no draft legislation yet. "There's not a lot of time sensitivity, but we're looking at introducing them in spring, hopefully for debate in the next two sessions next year," a spokesman for Kemp said. Kemp's office said the measures may be contained in two or three different bills, but was unsure as to the detail at this stage.
Impact on revenue: minus A$24 million, minus A$50 million.
TAX CRACKDOWN on income injected into loss-making trusts.
TAX CRACKDOWN on company profits disguised as loans.
TAX CRACKDOWN on foreign-sourced income.
The programme for enacting these measures is unknown.
Impact on revenue: A$7 million, A$215 million.
NATIONAL CRIME AUTHORITY INVESTIGATIONS of "complex money-laundering and tax evasion schemes".
It is unclear whether this police action requires any new legal authority. Government offices were unable to give details.
Impact on revenue: Zero, A$40 million. ----------------------
SPENDING MEASURES:

SAVINGS INCENTIVES -- The government will replace the former government's superannuation contribution with a cheaper tax break on savings. Abolition of the formerly programmed government payments will presumably be included in the other savings legislation, discussed above.
Savings: minus A$1 million, A$1.08 billion.

DRUGS SUBSIDIES -- The government will cut the cost of medical subsidies by paying a fixed amount for each group of therapeutic products. This is a regulation instrument and therefore, requires no legislation. The changes are scheduled to take place in March 1998.
Savings: A$44 million, A$167 million.

INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY -- A rationalisation of the government's computer budget. This is an administrative measure where computer requirements are being outsourced on a contract basis. It does not require legislation and the process has already started.
Savings: Zero, A$38 million.
CHILDCARE -- Limits on new places. New legislation is required and will be introduced into parliament in the next two weeks. Debate is expected to take place in the spring session.
Savings: A$10 million, A$42 million.

RENT ASSISTANCE -- Removal of a double subsidy. To take effect from January 1, 1998. The legislation will probably be introduced into parliament in the next two weeks and debated in the spring session. A spokesman for Social Security Minister Jocelyn Newman said he did not know if the legislation had been drafted yet.
Savings: A$21 million, A$58 million.

RURAL ADJUSTMENT SCHEME -- Will be wound down until September 30, 1997 and will be replaced by an integrated rural policy package, which will be announced in October 1997. A spokesman for Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said he believed there would be some legislative requirements involved in winding up the scheme but unsure about the detail at this stage.
Savings: A$46 million, A$44 million.

FEDERAL STATE HOUSING DEAL -- New funding arrangements. This measure does not require legislation. Funding arrangements are discussed with the state premiers in the context of the Council of Australian Governments (COAG).
Savings: A$50 million, A$50 million.

DEFERRED RETIREMENT BONUS -- Money for people who defer retirement. To take effect in July 1998 so no legislation drafted at this time. Legislation is likely to be introduced and debated in the spring session of parliament.
Savings: minus A$4 million, A$21 million.
SOCIAL SECURITY CRACKDOWN -- More data matching. To take effect in July 1998 with legislation expected to be debated in the spring session of parliament.
Savings: A$16 million, A$32 million.
HEALTH EFFICIENCIES -- Refocussing general practice. This is an administrative measure and therefore, requires no legislation. This streamlining procedure is already underway.
Savings: A$34 million, A$28 million.

PHARMACEUTICALS -- some items dropped from the free list. This measure is an instrument which does not require legislation. It happens on instruction from the government and is scheduled to take effect in March 1998.
Savings: A$12 million, A$31 million.
CHILDREN'S SERVICES PROGRAMME -- improved targetting. New legislation is required and will be introduced into parliament in the next two weeks. Debate is expected to take place in the spring session.
Savings: A$3 million, A$15 million.
GOVERNMENT PROPERTY MAINTENANCE -- Improved procedures, presumably requiring no legislation.
Savings: A$47 million, A$52 million.
TAX CRACKDOWN -- More data matching with social security. To take effect in July 1998 with legislation expected to be debated in the spring session of parliament.
Savings: A$28 million, A$27 million.
INDUSTRY JOBS SCHEME -- Abolished. No information available.
Savings: A$5 million, A$17 million.
VOCATIONAL EDUCATION -- Grants to states. No information available.
Savings: A$10 million, A$20 million.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FUNDING cut. This will be included in the routine appropriations authorisations which cannot be blocked without sparking a constitutional crisis.
Savings: A$391 million, A$575 million.

FEDERATION FUND -- A birthday present for the 100th anniversary of the federation of Britain's Australian colonies in 2001. A spokeswoman from Prime Minister John Howard's office said it was too early to know what legislative form this measure would take.
Savings: Zero, A$100 million.
OLYMPIC FUNDING boost. No special legislation required. Funding is done through appropriations.
Savings: A$4 million, A$63 million.
RURAL POLICY PACKAGE -- Will replace rural adjustment scheme with detail to be announced in October 1997.
Savings: A$45 million, A$46 million.
AUSTRALIAN FILM FINANCE CORPORATION -- Funding continued. No substantial changes so no legislation required.
Savings: Zero, A$48 million.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
